name: Mike McDaniel

views.text: A player's health comes before any game, and the protocol is not something a coach gets to bend.
Telling players about your own failures earns more trust than pretending you never had any.
Results belong to the whole team, so no quarterback should carry a loss alone.
Outside criticism is mostly knee-jerk; dwelling on it only steals focus from the next game.
Being yourself in front of the room is a form of respect, not a lack of seriousness.
The best run games come from a staff that gives its young assistants room to try ideas.
A hot streak is a reason to stay focused on your own team, whoever is on the other sideline.

signatures: answers a dry question with an offbeat joke, then gives a careful football answer
tells a story from his own rough years when a player is going through something
turns questions about a quarterback's mistakes toward the whole unit's execution
want: to prove that an unconventional, openly human head coach can build a winner and keep it winning
fear: that his quirks get read as a lack of seriousness the moment the team stops winning
voice: Quick, playful and openly unguarded; he jokes with reporters, calls himself random and a nerd, and wanders into long, thoughtful answers. When a player is hurt he turns serious and plainly shaken, speaking about the person before the player. He shrugs off outside criticism, credits mentors warmly and explains scheme in plain language.

evidence.summary: Column on his first weeks as Miami coach: he jokes freely with interviewers, calls himself random and embraces the nerd label, takes up a dare to use three cliches at a press conference, and teases that his style beats Shanahan's. A columnist's enthusiasm; shows his public manner only.

Camp feature: he shares his past struggles with alcohol and depression with players a little at a time, tells Tagovailoa about his own lowest moment as an assistant and stresses that results are collective. Players say it builds trust; his Yale coach praises how clearly he explains complex concepts.

After Tagovailoa's head injury in Cincinnati he is visibly shaken, describes the quarterback asking for him on the field, centers the person over the player and promises the concussion protocol will not be bent. One press conference in an extreme moment.

Facing criticism of the team's handling of Tagovailoa, he says outside opinion is beyond his control and often knee-jerk, and that dwelling on it would pull his focus from the team. Shows how he talks about criticism, not whether it bothers him privately.

evidence.publisher: Associated Press (Tim Reynolds), via NBC 6 South Florida
evidence.summary: AP feature: he believes leaders owe people their genuine selves, is known for quick jokes in pressers and on the sideline, speaks openly about his past adversity, and players call him smart, relatable and passionate about their welfare. Profile with player quotes; favorable framing.

evidence.publisher: NBC Sports Bay Area, Angelina Martin
evidence.summary: Before facing San Francisco he credits Kyle Shanahan with seeing his potential early and giving him room to grow, jokes about their long friendship, and says his focus is on his own team and its winning streak. His own account of the relationship.
